h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: Gradient noise from tiny batches compounds through three ReLU layers into instability, so larger batches help deep nets more than shallow ones.
Strong L2 applied across more layers over-shrinks multiplicative paths and pushes deep nets toward constant outputs.
Wider nets move the function faster per Adam step, partially substituting for a tiny step size within 243 epochs.
Large fan-in multiplies per-step pre-activation changes, so raising lr reaches instability sooner in wide nets.
Large batches give fewer, less noisy updates, so they both need and tolerate bigger steps.
Very wide nets carry excess capacity that overfits small tabular sets, so explicit decay is more useful there.
sklearn scales the L2 term by 1/batch_size, so at large batches raising alpha moves toward a useful strength rather than over-regularizing.
In three-layer nets parameters grow quadratically with width, adding instability and overfitting rather than needed capacity.
Narrow layers are a capacity bottleneck that an extra layer relieves through composition.
At tiny learning rates the net is step-starved, so cutting the number of updates with larger batches hurts most.
